To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

gap junctions in diseased myocardial tissue undergo remodelling, with changes in the distribution of gap and connexin types, and that these changes are associated with altered cardiac function and arrhythmogenesis.
remodelling of gap-junctional communication in the heart, in the form of altered expression and distribution of connexins, is a common and important feature of cardiac disease.

gap junctions and the connexins that comprise them are dynamic structures that undergo remodelling in diseased myocardial tissue, and that these changes are associated with altered electrical and mechanical behaviour.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of gap junctions in the heart and their involvement in disease, and is focused on three major questions: 1.
understanding how connexin expression is regulated and how the properties of the gap junctions that they form influence normal and abnormal electrical and mechanical function of the heart.
the molecular and structural bases for the functional properties of gap junctions in normal and diseased heart.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
connexin expression, gap junction organization and intercellular communication in the diseased heart is a very complicated and poorly understood area.

connexin expression, gap junction organization, connexin interactions and their functions are altered in cardiac disease, but the precise nature of these changes and their functional consequences are still being worked out.
connexins and their associated regulatory proteins are important in normal and abnormal cardiac function, and that much remains to be learned about their roles in health and disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the connexins are a complex and multifaceted family of proteins, and that their expression and organization are finely tuned to ensure the correct function of the heart.
the connexin/calcium hypothesis of arrhythmogenesis is a very attractive hypothesis, which is now being tested in detail.

connexin expression, connexin interactions with other proteins, and connexin-based gap junction organization are all dynamically regulated in response to pathological stimuli and that these processes play a significant role in the development of cardiac arrhythmias and other manifestations of heart disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that

connexins are not merely passive conduits of current flow, but rather that their expression and organization are dynamically and precisely controlled, and that connexins play an important role in determining the electrical and contractile properties of cardiac muscle.
the connexins and the gap junctions they make are key players in cardiac disease.
